segments.title: Pavageau gives his birth date and years on guitar and bass
segments.summary: Slow Drag Pavageau says he was born in 1888, played guitar 1906-27 and bass 1928-57, and mentions taking a soapbox.

segments.title: Soapbox bass demonstration and wrapping up the session
segments.summary: Russell and others try rubbing a broom, bottle and string to make a homemade bass sound; the talk turns to Dick Allen's tub bass and strings, and the session is closed.

segments.title: Marrero's banjo mute and an easy B-flat chord fingering
segments.summary: Marrero shows a mute and Allen works out Marrero's easy one-finger way to make a B-flat chord.

segments.title: Young white banjo players and the age of Marrero's banjo
segments.summary: Marrero offers to help Allen, talks about Bill Huntington and John Schaff, who play without knowing how to hold a banjo, and how old his instrument is.

segments.title: Previous owners of the banjo, instruction books and reading music
segments.summary: Frank Myers owned the banjo before; they look at Morris and McNeil method books, and Marrero says he plays mostly by ear and reads some.

segments.title: Brother John Marrero and how Marrero came to the banjo
segments.summary: Marrero says his brother John, who played with Celestin, Piron, Oliver and others, started him on banjo; his mother played guitar and his father and brother bass; he moved from guitar through bass to banjo and drums.

segments.title: McNeil's Progressive Studies and a trip to New York
segments.summary: Allen reads out details of McNeil's banjo studies published by Forster; Marrero briefly recalls a good time on a New York trip.

segments.title: Chord positions and playing guitar in the old days
segments.summary: Allen asks if Marrero uses the chords in the book; Marrero says in jazz you play whatever works, notes early guitar had no extended chords, and shows alternate positions for F.

segments.title: Basic chords for rhythm playing and chord sequences in different keys
segments.summary: Allen asks which chords matter most; Marrero explains relying on the ear, playing the blues in C, moving shapes up the neck, and chord progressions in several keys.

segments.title: Manetta as teacher and the Black and Tan band in the District
segments.summary: Marrero praises Manetta as a professor of music who plays two trumpets at once, and recalls playing at the Black and Tan on Abbeville and Burgundy with Manetta and Udell Wilson.

segments.title: Marrero's wrist action and his injured finger
segments.summary: Allen asks about Marrero's wrist work; Marrero explains his mattress-factory accident left him unable to use his first finger, so he holds the pick differently.

segments.title: Marrero's rhythm style and George Guesnon's teaching
segments.summary: Marrero describes himself as a solid band banjoist rather than a soloist, recalls a fine rhythm section, and praises George Guesnon, whom his brother taught.

segments.title: Seventh chords in different positions and getting a good tone
segments.summary: Marrero demonstrates seventh chords up the neck for Allen and stresses fingering right behind the fret for good tone.

segments.title: More chord demonstration, Huntington and Schaff, and the first recording with George
segments.summary: Marrero finishes the chord demonstration, talks again about Huntington and Schaff, and mentions wanting a band and the first recording made with George.

segments.title: Lumber yard and furniture store jobs
segments.summary: Marrero describes working at a furniture store and a lumber yard on the Industrial Canal before George called him back, and says he has not touched his banjo for a long time.

segments.title: Memories of the Beverly Cavern, his children, and closing remarks
segments.summary: Allen recalls hearing the band at the Beverly Cavern; Marrero says he has six living children out of sixteen, and the visit winds down with encouragement to Allen.

segments.title: The 1955 Boston trip, Tony Parenti and praise for George Lewis
segments.summary: They recall Parenti replacing George on the Boston trip in 1955, and Marrero calls George Lewis the greatest player and a generous man, then the tape ends.
